Introduction to BEJSON & Core Foundational Principles

The Architectural Philosophy of BEJSON

Modern data serialization formats are consistently forced into a trade-off between human legibility, machine parsing speed, schema safety, and payload efficiency. Traditional JSON (JavaScript Object Notation) excels in developer ubiquity and plain-text transparency, yet it introduces massive textual redundancy when serializing tabular or multi-record datasets. In a standard JSON array of objects, every attribute key is explicitly repeated across every single record row. For large datasets or high-density context windows in Large Language Model (LLM) prompts, this key repetition inflates storage footprints, increases network latency, and wastes critical token capacity.

Conversely, binary formats such as Protocol Buffers or Apache Avro achieve optimal byte compactness and parsing speeds, but they sacrifice plain-text readability, introduce heavy compilation toolchain dependencies, and require external schema files to decode payload contents. When an LLM or a light edge client encounters a raw binary stream, direct interpretation becomes impossible without runtime schema fetching and deserialization middleware.

BEJSON (BOEHNEN ELTON JSON) was engineered by Elton Boehnen to bridge this divide. BEJSON is a strict, self-describing tabular data standard constructed entirely on top of standard JSON syntax. By factoring out structural metadata—such as field names, primitive types, and relational scope—into top-level manifest arrays while maintaining row values in contiguous, order-bound tuples, BEJSON dramatically compresses plain-text representation while preserving instant readability. Crucially, BEJSON achieves high machine parsing performance by enforcing absolute positional integrity across its internal structures.

The Principle of Positional Integrity

At the core of the BEJSON specification lies positional integrity. Positional integrity dictates that the exact ordinal sequence of field definition objects inside the top-level Fields array strictly mirrors the physical value offsets within every row array contained in the Values matrix.

Formally, if a field definition object situated at index $i$ of the Fields array defines a property (e.g., {"name": "temperature", "type": "number"}), then for any record row $R$ within the Values matrix, the element $R[i]$ strictly corresponds to that property value. There are no inline key-value pairs inside record rows. Lookups transition from runtime key-string matching to $O(1)$ indexed array accesses.

BEJSON Positional Indexing Architecture:

Fields Array:   [0: "sensor_id"]  [1: "timestamp"]  [2: "temperature"]  [3: "is_active"]
                       │                 │                  │                  │
                       ▼                 ▼                  ▼                  ▼
Values Matrix:  [0: "S-101"]      [1: "17100000"]   [2: 23.8]          [3: true]
                [0: "S-102"]      [1: "17100060"]   [2: null]          [3: false]

By enforcing this structural constraint, runtime execution engines eliminate the computational expense of key re-parsing per record. A BEJSON parser scans the Fields definition exactly once to construct an internal, cached field-map lookup dictionary. Subsequent data extraction loops evaluate position offsets directly via numerical indices.

Runtime Indexing & Field Map Caching

To maximize programmatic processing speed across heterogeneous runtime environments (such as Node.js, Web Browsers, and Python runtimes), standard BEJSON runtime libraries implement an $O(1)$ Field Map Cache. The engine dynamically maps string keys to integer column offsets and attaches an internal reference (e.g., _bejson_field_map) to the document instance or maintains a thread-safe global cache map.

// Standard BEJSON Positional Indexing Engine (Reference Implementation)
function bejson_core_get_field_map(doc) {
    if (!doc || !doc.Fields) return {};

    // High-performance in-document cache check
    if (doc._bejson_field_map) return doc._bejson_field_map;

    const fieldMap = {};
    doc.Fields.forEach((field, index) => {
        fieldMap[field.name] = index;
    });

    // Inject hidden cache property for instantaneous sub-sequent lookups
    try {
        Object.defineProperty(doc, '_bejson_field_map', {
            value: fieldMap,
            writable: true,
            enumerable: false,
            configurable: true
        });
    } catch (e) {
        // Fallback for sealed/frozen objects
    }

    return fieldMap;
}

function bejson_core_get_field_index(doc, fieldName) {
    const fieldMap = bejson_core_get_field_map(doc);
    const idx = fieldMap[fieldName];
    return (idx !== undefined) ? idx : -1;
}

When traversing millions of records, the runtime resolves bejson_core_get_field_index(doc, "temperature") to a fixed offset (e.g., index 2). Row iterations then read row[2] directly, entirely bypassing native object key hashtable lookups.

The Six Mandatory Top-Level Keys

Every fully compliant BEJSON document—regardless of specific format version or specialized dialect—must contain exactly six mandatory top-level keys. The presence, exact casing, and structure of these keys form the invariant header contract that allows parsers and validators to immediately recognize, verify, and ingest BEJSON payloads without relying on external schema files.

Key Name Type Specification & Structural Invariants
Format string Must be strictly set to the exact literal value "BEJSON". Identifies the document as conforming to the Boehnen Elton JSON framework.
Format_Version string Must declare a valid format version dialect. Allowed standard core values are "104", "104a", or "104db".
Format_Creator string Must be set precisely to the string literal "Elton Boehnen". Acts as an immutable format origin and spec-compliance header.
Records_Type array An array of string identifiers declaring the entity types contained within the document. In single-entity formats (104, 104a), it must contain exactly one entity string. In multi-entity relational formats (104db), it contains two or more unique entity strings.
Fields array An array of field-definition objects establishing schema sequence, property names, data types, and structural bindings. Duplicate field names are explicitly forbidden.
Values array A matrix (array of arrays) representing data records. Every outer element is an array representing a record row. The element count of every row must strictly match the length of the Fields array. Missing or non-applicable values must be represented by explicit null padding.

Anatomy of a Canonical BEJSON Document

The following example demonstrates a fully compliant BEJSON document declaring a single entity type ("SystemMetric"). Notice how the tabular values maintain absolute length and positional alignment with the defined schema elements:

  ],

    },

    },

    },
    {

      "type": "integer"
    },
    {
      "name": "status_flags",
      "type": "array"
    }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [
      "NODE-EAST-01",
      "2026-09-24T08:30:00Z",
      42.75,
      8192,
      ["HEALTHY", "PRIMARY"]
    ],
    [
      "NODE-EAST-02",
      "2026-09-24T08:30:00Z",
      98.12,

    ],

Engineering Rationale: LLMs, Performance, and Self-Containment

BEJSON was specifically designed to meet three critical challenges in modem software engineering: artificial intelligence context optimization, deterministic machine processing, and complete schema self-containment.

1. Large Language Model (LLM) Context Optimization

When autonomous agents or LLM-based systems process database queries, API responses, or system state exports, token utilization is a primary constraint. Standard JSON objects consume unnecessary context window tokens by repeating key identifiers across every entry. For example, passing 1,000 records containing 10 fields each duplicates 10,000 string keys in prompt memory.

BEJSON eliminates key duplication, reducing text volume by 30% to 60% depending on field name lengths. Simultaneously, unlike binary formats, BEJSON remains 100% human-readable plain text. LLMs natively understand the tabular relationship between the header Fields array and the record rows in Values, enabling direct reasoning, logical filtering, and accurate modification of BEJSON payloads without requiring complex parsing tools.

2. Machine Parsing Performance & Predictability

Because every row array in Values guarantees a static length matching Fields.length, memory allocation during string parsing becomes linear and predictable. Parsers avoid dynamic object property allocation per row. Type checking is centralized: the data type asserted at Fields[j].type validates the literal at Values[i][j] across all rows $i$. Missing values are strictly encoded as null rather than omitted keys, ensuring structural predictability across all execution threads.

3. Explicit Schema Self-Containment

External schema files (such as .proto files or external .json schemas) introduce operational drift risks: if a application deployment updates its binary code without synchronizing its external schema repository, downstream parsers fail catastrophically. BEJSON documents carry their complete schema inline within the document header. A system receiving a raw BEJSON string can perform full structural validation, type enforcement, and relational mapping relying solely on the file's self-contained metadata.

By enforcing positional integrity, standardizing the mandatory top-level header contract, and optimizing plain-text representation, BEJSON establishes a resilient foundational standard for high-density, structured data exchange across modern computing environments.

BEJSON Format Specifications: 104, 104a, 104db, and Core Nesting

BEJSON 104: High-Throughput Single-Entity Serialization

The BEJSON 104 specification represents the foundation of the BEJSON dialect ecosystem. Designed primarily for high-density, single-entity record streams—such as operational telemetry, raw application logs, audit trails, and transactional event pipelines—version 104 establishes a strict, unadorned structural schema focused entirely on speed and raw throughput.

Structural Constraints and Dialect Invariants

BEJSON 104 imposes rigid constraints on document headers to eliminate overhead during stream parsing:

  • Single Entity Scope: The Records_Type array must contain exactly one string literal declaring the entity type (e.g., ["TelemetryPayload"]). Declaring multiple record types in a 104 document constitutes an immediate validation failure.
  • Header Strictness: Beyond the six mandatory top-level BEJSON keys (Format, Format_Version, Format_Creator, Records_Type, Fields, and Values), custom top-level keys are strictly prohibited. The parser will immediately reject documents containing unrecognised top-level property additions.
  • The Parent_Hierarchy Exception: The sole exception to the custom key restriction is the built-in, optional Parent_Hierarchy key. This string key provides a standardized relative path mechanism used by multi-file database systems to establish lineage to an owning manifest file (e.g., "Parent_Hierarchy": "../104a.mfdb.bejson").
  • Rich Type System Support: Unlike primitive-restricted variants, BEJSON 104 fully supports complex nested JSON structures. Allowed field types include string, integer, number, boolean, array, and object.
{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Parent_Hierarchy": "../104a.mfdb.bejson",
  "Records_Type": [
    "SensorTelemetry"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "device_id", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "reading_timestamp", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "metrics", "type": "object" },
    { "name": "error_codes", "type": "array" },
    { "name": "is_calibrated", "type": "boolean" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [
      "DEV-9082",
      "2026-09-24T10:15:00Z",
      { "voltage": 12.4, "amperage": 1.15, "temp_c": 41.2 },
      [0, 104],
      true
    ],
    [
      "DEV-9083",
      "2026-09-24T10:15:01Z",
      { "voltage": 11.9, "amperage": 0.98, "temp_c": 38.7 },
      null,
      true
    ]
  ]
}

BEJSON 104a: Primitive Metadata & Manifest Architecture

While version 104 optimizes for rich tabular payload execution, BEJSON 104a is engineered explicitly for high-speed configuration management, manifest registration, state metadata, and operational health checks. It trades complex nested data structures for lightweight processing speed and extensible document-level metadata.

Primitive Type Boundaries

To guarantee zero-recursion parsing passes, BEJSON 104a explicitly forbids complex data structures inside its Fields array. Every field definition in a 104a document must belong strictly to one of four primitive data types:

  1. string
  2. integer
  3. number
  4. boolean

Attempting to register a field with a type of array or object in a 104a document triggers a hard type-registration error. This primitive constraint allows 104a parsers to process records with deterministic memory allocations and flat byte-scanning algorithms.

Extensible Document-Level Header Metadata

Unlike versions 104 and 104db, BEJSON 104a allows custom top-level keys to be declared alongside the mandatory header contract. These keys serve exclusively as file-level or database-level metadata and must never be used to store row-level record values.

Custom metadata keys in 104a must adhere to strict architectural rules:

  • PascalCase Naming Convention: All custom header keys must be structured in PascalCase (e.g., Schema_Version, Network_Role, Retention_Days) to visually distinguish file metadata from internal record fields.
  • Reserved Namespace Protection: Custom keys must never collide with the six mandatory header keys or reserved operational headers (e.g., Parent_Hierarchy).
  • Single Entity Binding: Like version 104, Records_Type must remain an array containing exactly one entity type string.
{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104a",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Schema_Name": "Cluster-Manifest",
  "Schema_Version": "2.1.0",
  "Environment": "Production",
  "Node_Count": 3,
  "Records_Type": [
    "NodeConfig"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "node_name", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "internal_ip", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "max_connections", "type": "integer" },
    { "name": "failover_enabled", "type": "boolean" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [ "edge-01", "10.0.4.11", 5000, true ],
    [ "edge-02", "10.0.4.12", 5000, true ],
    [ "edge-03", "10.0.4.13", 2500, false ]
  ]
}

BEJSON 104db: Single-File Multi-Entity Relational Storage

The BEJSON 104db dialect solves a fundamental challenge in file-based persistence: representing multi-entity relational schemas within a single, atomic text document without breaking LLM readability or positional integrity.

Where traditional databases require binary tables or multiple linked files, BEJSON 104db encodes heterogeneous tables into a unified Values matrix using single-table inheritance semantics, strict field attribution, and positional null-padding.

1. The Discriminator Field & Mandatory Header Alignment

A BEJSON 104db document explicitly declares two or more unique entity string identifiers within its top-level Records_Type array (e.g., ["Customer", "Invoice", "LineItem"]). Custom top-level metadata headers are strictly prohibited in 104db.

To establish unambiguous row-level entity binding, the specification mandates that the very first object in the Fields array (position 0) must be the entity discriminator field defined precisely as:

{ "name": "Record_Type_Parent", "type": "string" }

For every record row present in the Values matrix, position 0 must contain a valid string matching one of the entities declared in Records_Type. If a row contains an unknown discriminator or a null value at index 0, the document fails structural validation.

2. Explicit Property Attribution & Positional Null-Padding

Every field definition within the Fields array (from index 1 onwards) must explicitly contain a Record_Type_Parent attribute mapping that field to its owner entity type:

{ "name": "credit_limit", "type": "number", "Record_Type_Parent": "Customer" }

There are no shared or "common" fields in 104db. If multiple entities require a concept such as created_at, separate field objects must be defined for each entity (e.g., customer_created_at bound to Customer, and invoice_created_at bound to Invoice).

Because all fields across all declared entities reside in a single master Fields array, individual record rows must utilize explicit null padding for all field positions that do not belong to their active Record_Type_Parent entity:

104db Memory Layout (Unified Matrix with Positional Null-Padding):

Field Index:    [0]                  [1]                 [2]                 [3]                  [4]
Field Name:     Record_Type_Parent   customer_id         company_name        invoice_id           invoice_total
Entity Binding: (Discriminator)      (Customer)          (Customer)          (Invoice)            (Invoice)
──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
Row 0 (Customer): "Customer"          "CUST-101"          "Acme Corp"         null                 null
Row 1 (Customer): "Customer"          "CUST-102"          "Globex Ltd"        null                 null
Row 2 (Invoice):  "Invoice"           null                null                "INV-9001"           1450.50
Row 3 (Invoice):  "Invoice"           null                null                "INV-9002"           820.00

3. Relational Foreign Keys (_fk Convention)

Relationships between distinct record types inside a 104db document are established through shared logical identity fields. By standard convention, foreign key fields utilize an _fk suffix pointing to the target entity's primary identity key (e.g., customer_id_fk bound to the Invoice entity, referencing customer_id on the Customer entity).

{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104db",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Records_Type": [
    "Customer",
    "Invoice"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "Record_Type_Parent", "type": "string" },
    
    { "name": "customer_id", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Customer" },
    { "name": "company_name", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Customer" },
    
    { "name": "invoice_id", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Invoice" },
    { "name": "customer_id_fk", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Invoice" },
    { "name": "amount_due", "type": "number", "Record_Type_Parent": "Invoice" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [ "Customer", "C-801", "Nexus Tech", null, null, null ],
    [ "Customer", "C-802", "Vanguard Systems", null, null, null ],
    [ "Invoice", null, null, "INV-1001", "C-801", 4500.00 ],
    [ "Invoice", null, null, "INV-1002", "C-801", 1250.75 ],
    [ "Invoice", null, null, "INV-1003", "C-802", 9800.00 ]
  ]
}

Architectural Comparison Matrix

The following technical reference matrix summarizes the structural distinctions across the three primary BEJSON core specifications:

Specification Feature BEJSON 104 BEJSON 104a BEJSON 104db
Primary Target Use-Case High-throughput streams, raw logs, dense entity tables. Configurations, metrics, cluster manifests, health checks. Single-file relational databases, embedded LLM state stores.
Record Type Count Strictly exactly 1 entity string. Strictly exactly 1 entity string. Multiple entity strings (minimum 2).
Custom Top-Level Headers Forbidden (Except built-in Parent_Hierarchy). Allowed (Must be PascalCase file-level metadata). Strictly Forbidden.
Supported Data Types Full spectrum (Primitives, array, object). Primitives only (string, integer, number, boolean). Full spectrum (Primitives, array, object).
Discriminator Field Requirement None. None. Mandatory Record_Type_Parent at Fields[0].
Field Attribution Property None. None. Mandatory Record_Type_Parent on all field definitions.
Null-Padding Rationale Used solely for missing or optional record data. Used solely for missing or optional record data. Mandatory structural padding across unowned field positions.

BEJSON Core Nesting: Embedded Tabular Structures

When engineering complex relational hierarchies, forced relational joins across separate flat tables can introduce unnecessary processing overhead. The BEJSON Core Nesting protocol allows fully formed, standard BEJSON 104 documents to be embedded directly within individual cell values of a parent 104 document while maintaining validation rigor and positional integrity.

1. Physical Coordinate Address Architecture (NestAddress)

Core Nesting eliminates the requirement for explicit foreign key declarations at the nested cell layer. Instead, child documents inherit implicit relational context derived directly from their physical storage coordinates in the parent container.

Every nested cell location is uniquely resolved via an explicit coordinate tuple:

$$\text{NestAddress}(\text{parent\_fp}, \text{row}, \text{col}, \text{depth})$$
  • parent_fp: The file path or system identifier of the root parent container.
  • row: The zero-based integer row offset inside the parent Values matrix.
  • col: The zero-based integer column index corresponding to the parent Fields position.
  • depth: The current recursive depth level (where root level = 0, embedded level = 1).

This physical addressing scheme allows child documents to establish deterministic relationships to parent rows without requiring synthetic surrogate key fields (such as parent_id) inside the child schema.

{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Records_Type": [
    "PlayerCharacter"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "player_id", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "character_name", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "inventory_bag", "type": "object" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [
      "PLYR-001",
      "Valerius",
      {
        "Format": "BEJSON",
        "Format_Version": "104",
        "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
        "Records_Type": [
          "InventoryBag"
        ],
        "Fields": [
          { "name": "item_id", "type": "string" },
          { "name": "quantity", "type": "integer" },
          { "name": "is_equipped", "type": "boolean" }
        ],
        "Values": [
          [ "ITEM-SWORD-09", 1, true ],
          [ "ITEM-POTION-01", 5, false ]
        ]
      }
    ]
  ]
}

2. Column-Schema Uniformity & Rule E134 Enforcement

To prevent structural drift across table cells, Core Nesting enforces strict Column-Schema Uniformity. If a parent column (e.g., inventory_bag at column index 2) contains nested BEJSON documents across multiple row entries, every nested document residing within that specific column must adhere to an identical field schema.

Specifically, across all nested documents in the same column:

  1. The sequence of field names in Fields must match precisely.
  2. The declared data types for every field index must be identical.
  3. The primary Records_Type identifier must remain consistent.

If row 0 contains a nested document with fields ["item_id", "quantity"] and row 1 embeds a document in the same column with fields ["item_id", "item_name", "quantity"], the nesting validator raises a hard structural exception: Error Code 134 (E134_SCHEMA_MISMATCH). This rule guarantees that query engines can process nested column arrays with uniform vector expectations.

3. Dotted-Path Navigation Grammar

Traversing deeply nested BEJSON structures is accomplished using a lightweight, standardized dotted-path grammar. The syntax allows execution engines to navigate arbitrarily deep embedded tabular cell hierarchies:

Dotted-Path Syntax Grammar:
[parent_field_name].[array_wildcard_or_index].[nested_field_name]

Examples:
1. inventory_bag[*].item_id      --> Resolves an array of all item_ids across all nested rows.
2. inventory_bag[0].quantity     --> Extracts the quantity field strictly from row 0 of the nested document.
3. character_attributes.stats[1].base_value --> Recursively traverses depth level 1 to level 2.

4. Safe Mutation & Depth Limits

When updating or appending records to an embedded BEJSON document, runtime engines must maintain absolute positional stability:

  • Append-Only Schema Evolutions: Modifying a nested document schema requires appending new properties exclusively to the end of the nested Fields array. Modifying or reordering existing field indices invalidates the column schema across all sister rows.
  • In-Place Null-Padding: If a new field is appended to a nested schema in row $r$, all other nested documents residing in the same parent column across all rows must immediately be null-padded at that new field position to satisfy Column-Schema Uniformity.
  • Maximum Recursion Safety Ceiling: To prevent stack overflows and memory exhaustion during recursive parsing, Core Nesting establishes a hard safety ceiling defined by the constant NESTING_MAX_DEPTH = 16. Documents attempting to embed structures beyond 16 recursive depth layers trigger an unrecoverable validation error.
  • Type Naming Conventions: The Records_Type declared inside an embedded 104 document should adopt the PascalCase representation of its parent column name (e.g., column inventory_bag embeds Records_Type: ["InventoryBag"]). Deviating from this convention produces an architectural standardization warning during validation audits.

Multi-File Database (MFDB) Architecture & Master-Slave Federation

MFDB Physical Architecture & File-System Layout

While single-file BEJSON dialects such as 104db provide unified multi-entity storage, expanding datasets or high-concurrency environments require physical file segregation. The Multi-File Database (MFDB) architecture layers directly on top of BEJSON core specifications (versions 104 and 104a), federating isolated table files into a single, cohesive relational database without breaking plain-text readability, LLM context isolation, or file-level lock granularity.

An MFDB database strictly decouples the database registry from individual entity tables across physical disk layouts:

Standard MFDB Physical Disk Layout:

mydb_root/
├── 104a.mfdb.bejson          ← Central Manifest Registry (BEJSON 104a)
└── data/                     ← Default Entity Storage Subdirectory
    ├── user.bejson           ← "User" Entity Table (BEJSON 104)
    ├── order.bejson          ← "Order" Entity Table (BEJSON 104)
    └── order_item.bejson     ← "OrderItem" Entity Table (BEJSON 104)

Every file residing within an MFDB layout is a completely valid, standalone BEJSON document. The system achieves database-level coherence through three architectural invariants:

  1. Manifest Anchor Invariant: The database root directory must contain exactly one central manifest file named strictly 104a.mfdb.bejson. Nested manifests within subdirectories are explicitly forbidden.
  2. Single-Entity Dense Storage: Every table inside the data/ subdirectory represents exactly one entity type serialized in BEJSON 104 format. Unlike BEJSON 104db, entity tables in MFDB do not utilize structural cross-entity null-padding; records are dense, and a null value denotes a genuinely absent attribute.
  3. Relative Lineage Pointer: Every entity file contains a mandatory top-level header key, Parent_Hierarchy, storing a relative POSIX file path pointing from the entity file's physical directory back to the central manifest.

The Manifest and Entity File Contracts

1. The Central Manifest Registry (104a.mfdb.bejson)

The manifest acts as the central directory, schema registry, and topological authority for the database. It is formatted strictly as a BEJSON 104a document and must comply with the following structural constraints:

  • Records_Type must be exactly ["mfdb"].
  • Format_Version must be "104a".
  • Standard PascalCase metadata headers must include MFDB_Version (e.g., "1.31") and DB_Name. Optional headers include DB_Description, Schema_Version, Author, Created_At, and Network_Role.
  • The Fields array must include two mandatory primitive fields: entity_name (string) and file_path (string). Standard optional fields include description (string), record_count (integer), schema_version (string), and primary_key (string).
{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104a",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "MFDB_Version": "1.31",
  "DB_Name": "EnterpriseLogistics",
  "Schema_Version": "1.2.0",
  "Network_Role": "Master",
  "Records_Type": [
    "mfdb"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "entity_name", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "file_path", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "description", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "record_count", "type": "integer" },
    { "name": "schema_version", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "primary_key", "type": "string" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [ "Customer", "data/customer.bejson", "Registered clients", 1250, "1.0", "customer_id" ],
    [ "Shipment", "data/shipment.bejson", "Active freight orders", 3420, "1.1", "shipment_id" ]
  ]
}

2. Individual Entity Tables (BEJSON 104)

Entity files store the actual row data for a specific table. Formatted as BEJSON 104 documents, they support rich types (including nested array and object fields) while adhering to strict lineage tracking:

{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Parent_Hierarchy": "../104a.mfdb.bejson",
  "Records_Type": [
    "Shipment"
  ],
  "Fields": [
    { "name": "shipment_id", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "customer_id_fk", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "origin_code", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "destination_code", "type": "string" },
    { "name": "waypoints", "type": "array" },
    { "name": "is_delivered", "type": "boolean" }
  ],
  "Values": [
    [
      "SHP-9001",
      "CUST-101",
      "KORD",
      "EGLL",
      [ "KORD", "CYQX", "EGLL" ],
      false
    ]
  ]
}

File-Local Discovery & Bidirectional Path Verification

A critical advantage of the MFDB specification is instant, file-local role discovery. A runtime engine or inspection tool encountering any isolated .bejson file on disk can deterministically establish its database role without performing broad file-system tree scans.

File-Local Discovery Algorithm

                                  ┌──────────────────────────┐
                                  │  Inspect Target File     │
                                  └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                               │
                                  ┌────────────▼─────────────┐
                                  │   Parse Top-Level JSON   │
                                  └────────────┬─────────────┘
                                               │

Bidirectional Path Verification

To prevent corrupt state, broken directory symlinks, or orphaned table files, MFDB validation engines enforce strict Bidirectional Path Verification during database mounting and integrity checks:

$$\text{Path}_{\text{Manifest}\to\text{Entity}} \equiv \text{Resolve}(\text{Dir}(\text{ManifestPath}), \text{Row}_{\text{file\_path}})$$ $$\text{Path}_{\text{Entity}\to\text{Manifest}} \equiv \text{Resolve}(\text{Dir}(\text{EntityPath}), \text{Entity}_{\text{Parent\_Hierarchy}})$$

Validation passes if and only if $\text{Path}_{\text{Manifest}\to\text{Entity}}$ resolves to the exact physical file location on disk, and that target entity's $\text{Path}_{\text{Entity}\to\text{Manifest}}$ resolves back to the original manifest file. If a file move alters relative directory depths without updating `Parent_Hierarchy`, the validation pipeline rejects the database, throwing hard error code E38 (E_MFDB_BIDIRECTIONAL_FAIL).

Master-Slave Federation & Unidirectional Data Streams

MFDB v1.31 introduces a federated multi-node protocol designed specifically to optimize LLM context window efficiency. By declaring the top-level Network_Role header in the central manifest, database instances operate in either "Master" or "Slave" topological roles.

Federation Node Role Topological Responsibility LLM Context Strategy I/O Privileges
Master Node Administrative authority, policy distribution, global audit logging, long-term data distillation. Full system visibility; retains macro-level index and cross-slave registry maps. Full Read/Write across global drop-zones and connected slave nodes.
Slave Node High-performance local operational workspace. Execution engine for localized tasks. Structural Blindness: Zero awareness of Master pathing or sister slaves; minimal context footprint. Restricted to local directory; emits telemetry exclusively via outbound drop-zones.

Active Communication Protocols

To maintain absolute context isolation on Slave nodes while preserving centralized control on the Master node, federated MFDB environments execute two distinct unidirectional communication patterns:

  1. One-Way Log Distillation (Slave $\to$ Master): As operational logs grow within a Slave's local entity tables (e.g., local execution traces), the Slave runs an automated distillation process (mfdb_federation_distill_logs). Local log tables are truncated to a fixed row ceiling (e.g., keeping only the last 100 rows), while overflow records are packaged into a standalone summary document and written out to the Master's polling directory drop-zone.
  2. Inverse Drop-Zone Polling & Atomic Swaps (Master $\to$ Slave): When the Master node pushes updated schema definitions, configuration manifests, or operational directives down to a Slave, it formats the update as a standard BEJSON document and writes it directly to a temporary drop-zone file within the Slave's directory. Once completely written, the Master executes an OS-level atomic file swap (e.g., fs.renameSync), replacing the active file instantaneously. This prevents partial-read race conditions on the Slave runtime.

1. In-Document Direct Cache Slot

When bejson_core_get_field_map(doc) evaluates a document, it first checks for the presence of an un-serialized runtime key: doc._bejson_field_map. If populated, the engine returns this object reference immediately, guaranteeing $O(1)$ attribute lookups across thousands of iterative queries.

2. Global Composite String Cache

If the document object lacks an internal reference (e.g., immediately after native JSON.parse() instantiation), the engine checks the process-global _FIELD_MAP_CACHE Map. The global cache key is computed by concatenating the format version with a CSV string of all ordered field names:

$$\text{CacheKey} = \text{Format\_Version} \mathbin{\Vert} \text{":"} \mathbin{\Vert} \sum_{i=0}^{N-1} \text{Fields}[i].\text{name} \mathbin{\Vert} \text{","}$$

Upon a global cache hit, the pre-built mapping is injected into doc._bejson_field_map for subsequent direct hits. If a document's Fields array is mutated dynamically during execution, the application must invoke bejson_core_clear_field_map_cache() to flush global maps and prevent index misalignment.

// Core JavaScript Implementation of Field Map Caching
function bejson_core_get_field_map(doc) {
    if (!doc || !doc.Fields) return {};

    // 1. Direct in-document O(1) hit
    if (doc._bejson_field_map) return doc._bejson_field_map;

    // 2. Global composite key lookup
    const fieldNames = doc.Fields.map(f => f.name);
    const cacheKey = (doc.Format_Version || '104') + ':' + fieldNames.join(',');

    let fieldMap;
    if (_FIELD_MAP_CACHE.has(cacheKey)) {
        fieldMap = _FIELD_MAP_CACHE.get(cacheKey);
    } else {
        fieldMap = {};
        doc.Fields.forEach((f, i) => { fieldMap[f.name] = i; });
        _FIELD_MAP_CACHE.set(cacheKey, fieldMap);
    }

    // Inject direct reference into target document instance
    try { doc._bejson_field_map = fieldMap; } catch (e) {}
    return fieldMap;
}

Field-Level AES-GCM Cryptography & Key Cache Management

BEJSON provides native cell-level and record-level confidentiality through authenticated AES-GCM (256-bit) encryption via the Web Crypto API, preserving tabular record structure while obfuscating sensitive payloads.

1. Encrypted Cell Serialization Format

When a record field is encrypted using CryptoUtils.encryptRecord(), primitive cell values are replaced in-place with a standard JSON descriptor object, preserving the positional array bounds of the row:

  "_enc": "AES-GCM",
  "salt": "u3xK...9aQ==",
  "iv": "d1F4...k2A==",
  "ct": "8xP2...m9N=="

Top-level discriminator headers (such as Record_Type_Parent) and the compliance key is_encrypted are explicitly exempted from field-level cipher transformations to keep structural query routing operational.

2. Key Derivation & The 12-Slot LRU Key Cache

Cryptographic keys are derived from user-supplied passwords and a 16-byte random salt using PBKDF2 configured for 100,000 iterations over SHA-256. Because deriving PBKDF2 keys on every row during bulk record iteration introduces unacceptable computational latency, the runtime maintains an internal 12-slot Least Recently Used (LRU) Key Cache (_KEY_CACHE_MAX_SLOTS = 12).

// 12-Slot LRU Key Cache Implementation
const _KEY_CACHE_MAX_SLOTS = 12;
const _keyCache = [];

async function _getOrDeriveKey(password, salt, providedKey = null) {
    if (providedKey) return providedKey;
    const saltB64 = CryptoUtils.ab2base64(salt);
    
    // Check LRU Cache Hit
    const hitIdx = _keyCache.findIndex((e) => e.password === password && e.salt === saltB64);
    if (hitIdx !== -1) {
        const [hit] = _keyCache.splice(hitIdx, 1);
        _keyCache.push(hit); // Promote to Most Recently Used
        return hit.key;
    }

    // Derive PBKDF2 Key on Miss
    const key = await CryptoUtils.deriveKey(password, salt);
    if (_keyCache.length >= _KEY_CACHE_MAX_SLOTS) {
        _keyCache.shift(); // Evict Least Recently Used
    }
    _keyCache.push({ password, salt: saltB64, key });
    return key;
}

Memory & File System Security Protocols

Deploying BEJSON and MFDB runtimes in untrusted or multi-tenant environments requires robust defensive controls against common injection vectors, path traversals, and concurrency bugs.

1. Prototype Pollution Prevention

When state management engines (such as BEJSONState) apply partial updates or restore dynamic historical snapshots, malicious object keys can compromise the host JavaScript process by overwriting Object.prototype. The engine enforces strict sanitization through a reserved blocklist Set (_DANGEROUS_KEYS):

const _DANGEROUS_KEYS = new Set(["__proto__", "constructor", "prototype"]);

function _sanitizeObject(obj) {
    if (obj === null || typeof obj !== "object" || Array.isArray(obj)) return obj;
    const safe = Object.create(null);
    for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) {
        if (_DANGEROUS_KEYS.has(k)) continue;
        safe[k] = _sanitizeObject(v);
    }
    return safe;
}

2. Path Traversal & Zip Slip Guards

To prevent malicious archive structures or path references from escaping designated workspace roots during unchunking or extraction, all file-system utilities invoke pure-JS POSIX path normalizers (secure_zip_validate). Path resolution rules enforce three security checks:

  1. Segment Scanning: Path segments are split by canonical separators and verified against __proto__, constructor, and prototype keys.
  2. Boundary Assertion: The target directory is normalized with an explicit trailing separator (targetWithSep). Resolved entry paths must satisfy an absolute prefix boundary check: $$\text{StartsWith}(\text{ResolvedEntryPath}, \text{TargetDir} \mathbin{\Vert} \text{sep}) \equiv \text{true}$$
  3. Environment Abstraction: Web environments employ a stack-based POSIX segment resolver to strip relative .. traversals without relying on native Node.js path bindings.
function secure_zip_validate(zip, targetDir) {
    const normalizeAbs = _nodePath ? (p) => _nodePath.resolve(p) : (p) => _normalizePath(p);
    const targetPath = normalizeAbs(targetDir);
    const sep = _nodePath ? _nodePath.sep : '/';
    const targetWithSep = targetPath.endsWith(sep) ? targetPath : targetPath + sep;

    zip.getEntries().forEach(entry => {
        const entryName = entry.entryName;
        const parts = entryName.replace(/\\/g, '/').split('/');
        
        for (const part of parts) {
            if (_DANGEROUS_KEYS.has(part)) {
                throw new Error(`Zip Slip (proto key): "${entryName}" contains a forbidden path segment`);
            }
        }

        const entryPath = _nodePath
            ? _nodePath.resolve(targetPath, entryName)
            : _normalizePath(targetPath + '/' + entryName);

        if (!entryPath.startsWith(targetWithSep) && entryPath !== targetPath) {
            throw new Error(`Zip Slip detected: "${entryName}" attempts to escape target directory`);
        }
    });
    return true;
}

3. Safe Atomic File Swapping

To ensure total transaction isolation during database mutations, manifest updates, or federated updates from Master nodes, the runtime prohibits writing directly to active files. Disk persistence executes via a 3-phase atomic swap sequence:

  1. Staging Write: Content is written to an isolated temporary file appended with process state and timestamp markers: destinationPath + ".tmp." + Date.now().
  2. Flush Verification: File contents are verified for complete byte writes and structural JSON integrity.
  3. Atomic OS Swap: The engine executes fs.renameSync(tempPath, destinationPath). On POSIX and Windows filesystems, this operation delegates to underlying OS kernel calls, guaranteeing that concurrent reader processes never observe partial or corrupted document states.

Architectural Benchmarks & LLM Context Optimization

Selecting an optimal persistence architecture requires evaluating token consumption, native execution dependencies, plain-text mutability, and relational performance. Traditional key-value JSON arrays repeat structural field keys across every record instance, introducing massive string redundancy. SQLite provides relational queries but relies on binary encodings that require external compiled drivers, rendering datasets unreadable to Large Language Models (LLMs) without intermediary extraction layers. BEJSON 104db and MFDB resolve this trade-off by decoupling schema declarations from row values while maintaining pure plain-text JSON standards.

LLM Context Readability High (Verbose) Zero (Binary File Format) Optimal (Dense Plain-Text)
Runtime Drivers Required Native JSON.parse() C Encoders / WASM Bindings Native JSON.parse()
Structural Key Redundancy $O(N \times F)$ Key Strings $O(1)$ Binary Page Headers $O(F)$ Declared Once in Header
Relational Modeling Manual Nested Arrays SQL Foreign Key Constraints Logical PK/FK via _fk Conventions

The primary advantage of BEJSON in AI-integrated pipelines is structural token compression. In standard JSON arrays of objects, every record duplicates every key name $F$ times for $N$ records. In BEJSON, keys are defined once within the top-level Fields array, reducing per-record payloads to positional primitive arrays.

The token overhead scaling for a dataset containing $N$ rows and $F$ fields can be formalized mathematically. Standard JSON scales token consumption according to key-value repetition:

$$T_{\text{Standard JSON}} \approx N \times \sum_{i=1}^{F} \left( \text{Tokens}(K_i) + \text{Tokens}(V_{i,j}) + C_{\text{syntax}} \right)$$

In contrast, BEJSON isolates key tokens into a single header declaration, scaling linearly strictly across value payloads:

$$T_{\text{BEJSON}} \approx \left( \sum_{i=1}^{F} \text{Tokens}(K_i) \right) + N \times \sum_{i=1}^{F} \left( \text{Tokens}(V_{i,j}) + C_{\text{delim}} \right)$$

As dataset length $N$ scales, the token compression ratio $R_{\text{context}}$ approaches:

$$R_{\text{context}} = \lim_{N \to \infty} \frac{T_{\text{Standard JSON}}}{T_{\text{BEJSON}}} = \frac{\overline{\text{Tokens}(K)} + \overline{\text{Tokens}(V)} + C_{\text{syntax}}}{\overline{\text{Tokens}(V)} + C_{\text{delim}}}$$

For datasets with average key lengths equal to or exceeding value lengths, BEJSON compresses context window usage by 40% to 65%, allowing LLMs to process significantly larger relational contexts within fixed window boundaries.

// Interactive State Management and Undo Pipeline
class BEJSONState {
    constructor(initialState = {}, options = {}) {
        initialState = _sanitizeObject(initialState) ?? {};
        this.schema_name = options.name || "BEJSONState";
        
        // Single-file multi-entity relational format initialization
        this.bejson = {
            Format: "BEJSON",
            Format_Version: "104db",
            Format_Creator: "Elton Boehnen",
            Records_Type: ["StateNode", "History"],
            Fields: [
                { name: "Record_Type_Parent", type: "string" },
                { name: "key", type: "string", Record_Type_Parent: "StateNode" },
                { name: "value", type: "string", Record_Type_Parent: "StateNode" },
                { name: "timestamp", type: "string", Record_Type_Parent: "History" },
                { name: "snapshot", type: "string", Record_Type_Parent: "History" }
            ],
            Values: []
        };

        this._fieldIdx = this._buildFieldIdx();
        this._historyIndex = -1;
        this.state = this._createProxy(initialState, '');
        
        this._syncToBEJSON();
        this._saveHistory();
    }

    _buildFieldIdx() {
        const fields = this.bejson.Fields;
        return {
            rtp:       fields.findIndex(f => f.name === "Record_Type_Parent"),
            key:       fields.findIndex(f => f.name === "key"),
            value:     fields.findIndex(f => f.name === "value"),
            timestamp: fields.findIndex(f => f.name === "timestamp"),
            snapshot:  fields.findIndex(f => f.name === "snapshot")
        };
    }

    _syncToBEJSON() {
        const fieldCount = this.bejson.Fields.length;
        const { rtp, key: keyIdx, value: valIdx } = this._fieldIdx;

        // Clear existing StateNode rows while preserving History
        this.bejson.Values = this.bejson.Values.filter(r => r[rtp] !== "StateNode");

        // Flatten active state key-value mapping into positional 104db rows
        for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(this.state)) {
            const row = new Array(fieldCount).fill(null);
            row[rtp] = "StateNode";
            row[keyIdx] = k;
            row[valIdx] = JSON.stringify(v);
            this.bejson.Values.push(row);
        }
    }

    _saveHistory() {
        const fieldCount = this.bejson.Fields.length;
        const { rtp, timestamp: tsIdx, snapshot: snIdx } = this._fieldIdx;

        const row = new Array(fieldCount).fill(null);
        row[rtp] = "History";
        row[tsIdx] = new Date().toISOString();
        row[snIdx] = JSON.stringify(this.state);

        this.bejson.Values.push(row);
        const historyRows = this.bejson.Values.filter(r => r[rtp] === "History");
        this._historyIndex = historyRows.length - 1;
    }

    undo() {
        const { rtp, snapshot: snIdx } = this._fieldIdx;
        const historyRows = this.bejson.Values.filter(r => r[rtp] === "History");
        
        if (this._historyIndex <= 0) return false;
        
        this._historyIndex--;
        const previousState = JSON.parse(historyRows[this._historyIndex][snIdx]);
        
        // Restore state safely after prototype sanitization
        const safe = _sanitizeObject(previousState) ?? {};
        Object.keys(this.state).forEach(k => delete this.state[k]);
        Object.assign(this.state, safe);
        this._syncToBEJSON();
        return true;
    }
}

Schema Evolution & Event Audit Protocols

Maintaining long-term compatibility in persistent BEJSON stores requires strict migration conventions. Because parsers evaluate array cells by numerical field offsets, structural changes must preserve positional integrity.

1. Non-Breaking Schema Additions (Append-Only Rule)

Adding new fields to an existing BEJSON schema is a minor, non-breaking evolution (e.g., updating Schema_Version from "1.0.0" to "1.1.0"). New field definitions must strictly append to the end of the Fields array. Legacy records encountered during parsing contain shorter length arrays than the updated field definition; runtimes safely hydrate missing trailing indexes as null without breaking field mapping lookups.

{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Parent_Hierarchy": "../104a.mfdb.bejson",
  "Records_Type": ["Customer"],
  "Fields": [
    {"name": "customer_id", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "email", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "loyalty_tier", "type": "string"}
  ],
  "Values": [
    ["C101", "alice@example.com", "Gold"],
    ["C102", "bob@example.com", null]
  ]
}

2. Breaking Schema Migrations

Removing a field, changing a field's primitive type, or inserting a field mid-array disrupts positional offsets. This constitutes a major breaking change requiring explicit migration workflows:

  • Manifest Version Increments: The Schema_Version in the 104a.mfdb.bejson manifest must increment its major semantic version.
  • Transactional Unchunking: The database workspace must be mounted via MFDB132Archive.mount() into an isolated directory.
  • Sequential Repackaging: Migration scripts load entity files, map existing values to transformed field structures, perform positional null-padding, and execute a pre-commit validation pass via mfdb_validator_validate_database() prior to invoked commit() calls.

3. The Event/Audit Discriminator Pattern

To record mutating operations, high-integrity BEJSON 104db and MFDB databases incorporate a dedicated "Event" entity type within the multi-entity manifest or discriminator headers. This pattern isolates immutable operational logs alongside core business entities while capturing full before-and-after change vectors inside structured object cells.

{
  "Format": "BEJSON",
  "Format_Version": "104db",
  "Format_Creator": "Elton Boehnen",
  "Records_Type": ["Account", "Event"],
  "Fields": [
    {"name": "Record_Type_Parent", "type": "string"},
    {"name": "account_id", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Account"},
    {"name": "balance", "type": "number", "Record_Type_Parent": "Account"},
    {"name": "event_id", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Event"},
    {"name": "related_entity_id_fk", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Event"},
    {"name": "action", "type": "string", "Record_Type_Parent": "Event"},
    {"name": "change_details", "type": "object", "Record_Type_Parent": "Event"}
  ],
  "Values": [
    ["Account", "ACC-901", 1250.50, null, null, null, null],
    ["Event", null, null, "EVT-8001", "ACC-901", "CREDIT_ADJUSTMENT", {"previous_balance": 1000.00, "new_balance": 1250.50, "author": "admin"}]
  ]
}

By enforcing positional field mappings, explicit foreign key conventions (_fk), and multi-entity discriminator padding, BEJSON provides a resilient, self-describing, plain-text relational foundation optimized for both programmatic performance and AI-native comprehension.
